primary_claim: Gradient-Routed Auxiliary Modules (GRAM), a modular pretraining method that isolates dual-use knowledge into switchable auxiliary modules trained in a single run, approximates the performance of separately trained data-filtered models across scales from 50M to 5B parameters, matches or exceeds LoRA and outperforms the post-hoc unlearning method MaxEnt on robustness to adversarial fine-tuning elicitation, and isolates capabilities better than both LoRA and data filtering when only 50% of training data is labeled.

models.family: custom dense Transformer (GRAM, trained from scratch)

effect.metric: compute-adjusted loss (Compute Ratio) on retained vs removed capabilities, and robustness to adversarial fine-tuning elicitation
effect.value: GRAM and LoRA closely track data-filtering performance on retained and removed capabilities at all 7 scales (50M-5B), at roughly a fifth of filtering's training compute; MaxEnt recovers to near all-data-baseline performance under adversarial fine-tuning (indicating suppression rather than removal), while GRAM, LoRA, and filtering remain robust

contradicts_or_qualifies: Qualifies MaxEnt, a post-hoc unlearning method, as not truly removing capabilities but only suppressing them, since it recovers to near-baseline performance after adversarial fine-tuning while GRAM, LoRA, and data filtering remain robust
stated_future_work: Scale modular pretraining to larger and more realistic settings
Figure out how to instruction-tune a model trained with GRAM
Better understand how modular pretraining works when data is imperfectly labeled, including when label errors aren't random and independent from the data
limitations_stated: Unclear whether entangled capabilities (e.g. general biology knowledge vs virology) make data filtering itself infeasible if they cannot be cleanly separated
Scaling trends verified only up to 5B parameters; unclear whether they continue at frontier scales or hold in a production setting
Experiments only use loss-based evals, which may not capture everything that matters for downstream tasks
LoRA with an optimized data mix is a strong baseline similar to GRAM and filtering in the main real-data setting, and the methods were not tested in meaningfully different settings
GRAM's advantages over LoRA (composability, partial-labeling isolation) rest on only two isolated experiments, so may not generalize
quote: GRAM approximates separately trained, data filtered models in a single run.
